title: Oxy-fuel Cutting — Theory and Safety Awareness
objective: Understand at knowledge level what oxy-fuel cutting is, where it fits within boilermaker fabrication, its broad material limitations, and why practical cutting requires authorised training and safety controls.

curriculum_traceability.primary_source: QCTO occupational curriculum hosted by CHIETA — Curriculum-6.pdf

safety_boundary: Theory and safety-awareness only. This lesson does not teach gas-cylinder connection, regulator or pressure settings, torch setup, ignition, flame adjustment, nozzle selection, cutting speed, torch movement, piercing, shutdown or how to perform oxy-fuel cutting. Practical cutting belongs in authorised occupational training under competent supervision.

sections.heading: 1. What oxy-fuel cutting is
sections.body: Oxy-fuel cutting is a thermal cutting process used in metal fabrication. At knowledge level, learners should recognise it as one of the cutting-process families encountered in boilermaker work.

sections.heading: 2. The underlying idea
sections.body: The process combines heating with an oxygen-driven reaction that enables suitable metal to be separated. Understanding this broad principle helps distinguish oxy-fuel cutting from other cutting families without teaching equipment operation.

sections.heading: 3. Material suitability matters
sections.body: Oxy-fuel cutting is particularly associated with suitable steels. Different metals respond differently to thermal cutting processes, so material identification and the approved fabrication specification matter before a cutting process is selected.

sections.heading: 4. Manual and mechanised contexts
sections.body: Oxy-fuel cutting can appear in manual and mechanised fabrication environments. The occupational learner should recognise these contexts while understanding that each requires appropriate equipment, controls, training and supervision.

sections.heading: 5. Quality requirements
sections.body: A cut component must ultimately meet the applicable drawing, dimensions, specification and quality requirements. Process choice does not replace inspection or authorised acceptance criteria.

sections.heading: 6. Safety awareness
sections.body: Thermal cutting environments can involve serious hazards including heat, fire, hot material, fumes and pressurised gases. Practical work therefore requires formal training, workplace controls, suitable protective measures and competent supervision.

sections.heading: 7. Process choice is controlled
sections.body: The appropriate cutting process depends on the material, drawing, specification, workplace procedure and available authorised equipment. Learners should understand the decision factors rather than independently selecting or operating cutting equipment.

sections.heading: 8. Stop and refer
sections.body: If the material, required cutting process, drawing, specification or approved procedure is unclear, stop and refer the matter to a competent trainer or supervisor before practical work is attempted.
